posts.title: Don't know where to start with AI? We got you
posts.subtitle: It’s insanely easy to get overwhelmed by AI. Every day a new tool drops on Facebook or Instagram promising magic. Here’s the truth: most of those apps are just pretty wrappers on the same few models you can already use—cheap or free. This guide cuts the noise and gets you hands‑on with a small set of tools that actually teach you how to think and build with AI.
posts.description: A beginner's guide to your first week in AI
posts.content:
What You’ll Get From This Guide

  • A short list of beginner‑friendly tools that cover research, learning, visuals, and media.
  • Exactly how to start with each one—first clicks, sample prompts, and small wins.
  • A realistic view of what’s hype vs. what’s real so you don’t waste money on wrapper apps.
  • A 30/60/90‑minute practice plan you can do this week, plus copy‑paste prompt templates.
Mindset rule: Learn a few impactful tools deeply. Ship tiny projects. Ignore the daily noise. You’ll progress faster than people chasing every shiny thing.

The Short List (Start Here)

We’ll focus on just five tools, each covering a different “mode” of working with AI:

  1. Manus AI — Agentic browser & doer. Give it a task; it opens a virtual computer, browses, clicks, fills forms, and reports back.
  2. NotebookLM — Your private study guide. Load your own sources (PDFs, docs, YouTube) and get summaries, Q&A, audio/ video overviews—grounded only in what you provided.
  3. ChatGPT / Google Gemini — Learn/Tutor modes — Guided learning. Use them as coaches that ask you questions and lead you to the answer instead of just blurting it out.
  4. NapkinAI — Auto‑visuals for talks & lessons. Paste text; it drafts engaging visuals that pair with your message.
  5. Generative media basics — Midjourney (images), Sora (video), Veo 3 (video). Describe what you want; get images/video drafts to iterate. (Availability, features, and limits vary by plan and region—always check your account.)
Note on paid plans: If you want one subscription: pick either ChatGPT or Gemini first. Both are excellent and frequently top benchmarks. Add others later if/when you need them.

Why wrappers feel magical (but usually aren’t)

A lot of viral apps promise “AI superpowers” but underneath they call the same public APIs you can access directly through ChatGPT, Gemini, or a handful of automation tools. Wrappers can be handy UI, but you often pay more for less control.

How to spot a wrapper:

  • The feature list looks like “generate X, summarize Y, rewrite Z” with no custom data, no unique model, and no export control.
  • Pricing that’s oddly high for the speed/quality you get.
  • No clear docs about which models they use or how your data is handled.

Rule of thumb: When in doubt, start with the core tools below. If a wrapper genuinely saves you time after you understand the basics—great. Otherwise, skip it.

Tool #1 — Manus AI (Agentic Browser & Doer)

What it is: Manus spins up its own sandboxed computer, opens a browser, and does things you ask—research, form‑filling, simple site creation/tests, scraping structured info, and more. It’s like giving a careful intern step‑by‑step instructions—except it can click, scroll, and type for you.

Why it matters: You learn the agentic pattern: turn fuzzy goals into stepwise plans the AI can execute, then check the output. This is the future of “let the computer do it,” and Manus is a hands‑on way to practice safely.

First 10 minutes:

  1. Create a task like: “Find three HVAC companies in Tulsa with at least 100 Google reviews; capture name, phone, website, and average rating into a CSV; share a summary.”
  2. Watch Manus open its workspace. It will browse, collect, and compile. You can see each step.
  3. Export the CSV and spot‑check 2–3 rows. Ask it to fix anything off.

Safety tips: Avoid tasks that require your real passwords or sensitive accounts. Keep projects in the public web and double‑check anything important.

Practice prompts:

  • “Research three competing roofing companies in Springfield. Provide a 5‑row table: company, pricing clues, specialties, review highlights, and website.”
  • “Find 5 authoritative sources on residential heat pump maintenance. For each: title, author, year, URL, and a 2‑sentence summary. Deliver Markdown.”

Small win (30 minutes): A clean competitor snapshot + CSV you can import into Sheets.

Tool #2 — NotebookLM (Your Private Study Guide)

What it is: A grounded research/learning tool. You upload your sources—PDFs (textbooks, manuals), Google Docs, pasted text, even YouTube links—and NotebookLM constrains answers to only those sources. It can also produce audio or video overviews that feel like a mini‑podcast or explainer for the exact material you provided.

Why it matters: This is real‑world retrieval‑based learning. No random internet guesses—just the text you trust, explained at your level. Perfect for students, onboarding, SOPs, and sermon/lesson prep.

First 10 minutes:

  1. Start a new Notebook called “Proverbs — Chapter 1.”
  2. Add your source: the text of Proverbs 1 (or your PDF chapter).
  3. Ask: “Explain this chapter in plain English. What’s the structure? What three themes should I remember?”
  4. Generate an audio overview and listen once through.

Study pattern that works:

  • Create one Notebook per chapter/module so context stays laser‑focused.
  • Use prompts like: “Quiz me on key terms, then show me what I missed.”
  • Ask for: “A one‑page summary, five comprehension questions, and two discussion prompts.”

Non‑student use cases:

  • Employee handbook: Upload your policies; generate a new‑hire “what to know this week.”
  • Onboarding docs: Turn a 20‑page SOP into a 5‑minute audio briefing.
  • Client prep: Summarize the last 6 meeting notes into a brief with action items.

Small win (30 minutes): One chapter mastered—summary, quiz, and a short audio overview you can replay.

Tool #3 — ChatGPT & Gemini Learn Modes (Guided Tutor)

What they are: Conversational models designed to teach, not just answer. They can coach you with questions, break concepts down, and pace explanations.

Why it matters: You’ll build the habit of clarifying your request and letting the model guide your understanding, instead of fishing for copy‑paste answers.

Parent/Student starter prompt (paste this at the top of a new chat):

“You are a patient tutor. Don’t give me final answers. Ask questions first to check what I know. Use simple language and short steps. If I’m stuck, give a hint or a smaller problem. Keep coaching until I can explain the answer back to you.”

Tutor flow that works:

  1. State your goal: “Help me understand ratios at a 6th‑grade level.”
  2. Give an example of where you got stuck.
  3. Ask for a 3‑question warm‑up. Answer. Get feedback. Repeat.

Small win (30 minutes): One concept you’ve always “sort of got” becomes second‑nature—because the model coached your thinking.

Tool #4 — NapkinAI (Auto‑Visuals for Talks & Lessons)

What it is: Paste a sermon, lesson, or presentation text; NapkinAI generates visuals that fit your words and help the message land.

Why it matters: Visuals are sticky. With almost no design effort, you’ll leave audiences with clearer takeaways.

First 10 minutes:

  1. Paste 300–600 words from your talk.
  2. Ask for: “3 visual slides: a metaphor opener, a process diagram, and a closing takeaway.”
  3. Export the set and tweak the labels.

Where it shines:

  • Teaching abstract concepts (for non‑technical audiences).
  • Sermons and youth talks that need a single strong image per idea.
  • Staff meetings where process clarity matters more than polish.

Small win (30 minutes): A three‑slide visual pack that matches your words.

Tool #5 — Generative Media Basics (Images & Video)

What they are:

  • Midjourney (images): Great for concept art, thumbnails, and brand mood.
  • Sora (video): Text‑to‑video generation from OpenAI (availability and limits vary—check your account).
  • Veo 3 (video): Google’s advanced text‑to‑video model (availability and limits vary—check your account).

Why it matters: Even if you never become a designer, you can put ideas on a canvas fast: moodboards, thumbnails, 5–10‑second clips for motion backgrounds or sermon bumpers.

Prompt pattern that works (images):

Subject + Style + Lighting + Composition + Use case
Example: “A minimal, high‑contrast hero image of a vintage printing press morphing into a modern laptop, cinematic rim lighting, 16:9, blog header.”

Prompt pattern that works (video):

Action + Setting + Camera moves + Mood/color + Length
Example: “10‑second shot of morning light over a quiet small‑town main street; slow dolly forward, warm tones, subtle motion blur.”

Reality check: Plans, features, and rate limits change. Treat these tools as creative accelerators, not final‑output factories. Expect to iterate.

Small win (30 minutes): One blog hero image and a 5–10 second clip for socials.

30 / 60 / 90‑Minute Starter Workouts

Pick one block this week. The goal is a concrete deliverable—not perfect, just shipped.

30 minutes — “Competitor Snapshot” (Manus + Sheets)

  • Manus task: “Find 3–5 competitors in my city with ≥100 Google reviews; collect name, site, phone, rating.”
  • Export CSV → open in Sheets → bold the top line.
  • Write 3 bullets: What stands out? What could we do better? One experiment for next week.

60 minutes — “Chapter Mastered” (NotebookLM)

  • Create a Notebook for one chapter/topic.
  • Generate summary, quiz, and audio overview.
  • Take the quiz cold, then after listening. Note what improved.

90 minutes — “Teach It Once, Use It Everywhere” (NapkinAI + Tutor Mode + Media)

  • Draft a 600‑word mini‑lesson with a Learn‑Mode chat.
  • Feed it to NapkinAI → get 3 visuals.
  • Create one Midjourney/Sora/Veo asset as the opener.
  • Save all assets to a folder named TopicName_LessonPack.

Copy‑Paste Prompt Pack (Use As‑Is)

Manus — Research → Table → CSV

“Open a new workspace. Research [topic]. Identify 5 reputable sources published within the last 3 years. For each, capture title, author/organization, year, URL, and a 2‑sentence summary. Deliver as a clean Markdown table and also export a CSV.”

NotebookLM — Study Sprint

“Using only the uploaded chapter, give me: (1) a 200‑word plain‑English summary, (2) 5 comprehension questions, (3) 2 discussion prompts, (4) a 90‑second audio overview script. Keep definitions concrete and examples specific.”

Tutor Mode — Socratic Coaching

“You are a patient tutor. Don’t give final answers. Ask what I know first, then guide me with 1–2 questions at a time. If I stall, offer a tiny hint. Keep explanations under 120 words. At the end, ask me to explain the concept back in my own words.”

NapkinAI — Visual Trio

“From this 500–700 word text, produce three visuals: (1) a metaphor opener image, (2) a 4‑step process diagram, (3) a one‑line takeaway poster. Keep labels short and legible for a projector.”

Generative Media — Blog Hero

“A split‑scene hero image: left side a 15th‑century wooden printing press in warm sepia; right side a modern laptop with a glowing AI chat interface in cool blue. A ribbon of letters morphs from metal type to digital tokens across the middle. Cinematic lighting, 16:9, no text.”

How to Evaluate Tools (Quick Framework)

Ask these five questions before you pay for anything:

  1. What model(s) does it actually use? If unclear, be cautious.
  2. Can I export my work easily? (Docs, CSV, images, video)
  3. Does it save me time every week? Try to quantify.
  4. Do I control my data? Read the privacy page, at least once.
  5. Can I do 80% of this with ChatGPT/Gemini + a simple workflow? If yes, skip the wrapper.

Troubleshooting & Gotchas

  • It “made stuff up.” Constrain the model: supply the source text (NotebookLM) or say “answer using only the quoted material.”
  • It’s too wordy. Add limits: “max 120 words,” “3 bullets only,” “6th‑grade reading level.”
  • It missed the point. Provide an example of “what good looks like,” then ask to match the style/structure.
  • It broke a website while browsing. Scale back the agent’s task. Give it smaller, clearer steps or switch sites.
  • Output looks bland. Ask for 3 alternate drafts in different tones, then mix and match.

FAQs

Do I need to code? No. Everything here is point‑and‑click. Coding helps later, but is optional.

Which single subscription first? Pick one: ChatGPT or Gemini, based on which interface you like and which features you actually use. You can build a lot with either.

Are Sora and Veo 3 available to everyone? Availability, features, and limits change. Check your plan and region inside your account; assume terms will evolve.

Is Manus safe to log into my accounts? Treat agentic browsing like you would a new assistant: don’t share sensitive credentials unless you fully understand the risks and sandbox.

What about all those viral “AI biz‑in‑a‑box” tools? Most repackage the same models. Learn the basics here first; you’ll quickly see which tools are worth it.

A Simple Plan For Your First Week

Day 1: Manus competitor snapshot → CSV → 3 takeaways.
Day 2: NotebookLM chapter study → summary + quiz + audio.
Day 3: Tutor mode on one stubborn concept → teach it back.
Day 4: NapkinAI visuals for a 5‑minute talk.
Day 5: One hero image or 10‑second clip for your next post.
Weekend: Pick your favorite result and share it. Teaching others locks in the skill.

Closing: Access Beats Elites—But Only If You Use It

You don’t need a hundred tools. You need a few that help you research, learn, explain, and create. Manus, NotebookLM, a Learn‑Mode chat (ChatGPT or Gemini), NapkinAI, and a basic image/video generator will take you from watching AI happen to making AI help. Ship one tiny project this week. Then another. Momentum beats perfection—every time.

posts.title: AI Is Our Printing Press Moment: Why Access Beats Elites
posts.subtitle: Why AI access is revolutionary for small businesses and creators
posts.description: When books became accessible, 'regular people' stopped waiting for gatekeepers and started building. AI is doing the same thing today - only faster, cheaper, and on a scale even Gutenberg couldn't dream of.
posts.content:
AI Is Our Printing Press Moment: Why Access Beats Elites

When books became accessible, "regular people" stopped waiting for gatekeepers and started building.

That was the printing press in the 15th century — the single invention that smashed the monopoly on knowledge.

Today, AI is doing the same thing. Only faster. Cheaper. And on a scale even Gutenberg couldn't dream of.

The Disruption Nobody Saw Coming

In the 1440s, Johannes Gutenberg invented a contraption that changed everything: movable type printing.

Before that, books were hand-copied by monks in candlelit rooms. Producing a single Bible could take years. Only the wealthy or the church could own one.

Gutenberg's press changed the math overnight:

  • From months to days. Hundreds of pages could be printed in a single day.
  • From elite to accessible. A middle-class family could own books for the first time.

And the ripple effects? You'd be surprised how far they went:

  • 📚 Science acceleration — For centuries, scientists worked in isolation. Now they could publish and share findings rapidly. Collaboration exploded.
  • ✝️ Religious transformation — Martin Luther's 95 Theses didn't just exist — they spread, copied and distributed widely, triggering the Reformation.
  • 🗣 Language standardization — Printed works made spelling and grammar more consistent, creating shared language norms across regions.
  • 📜 Business revolution — Contracts, price lists, and product catalogs could be mass-produced. The first scalable "content marketing" was born.

The printing press didn't just change how people read. It changed what was possible.

If you were alive in 1450, the printing press might not have looked revolutionary. It was a clunky machine in a workshop. But within a generation, the world was unrecognizable.

Today's AI tools feel the same way.

Why This Matters Now

AI is lowering the barrier to entry for every kind of knowledge work.

Tasks that took weeks can now take hours — or minutes.

Some examples:

  • Small businesses can automate customer emails, phone call scripts, and appointment scheduling.
  • Content creators can batch-create a month's worth of posts, videos, and graphics in one afternoon.
  • Designers and non-designers alike can create visuals from an idea in their head — no art degree required.
  • Data-heavy tasks like financial reporting or forecasting can be run in real-time with a single prompt.

And here's the key: the winners will be the ones who act now.

Waiting for AI to "settle down" is like a merchant in 1450 waiting to see if the printing press catches on.

Do This This Week (60–90 Minutes)

You don't need a "grand plan" to start. You just need one useful loop.

  1. Pick a tiny friction point.
    • Slow quotes?
    • Customers asking the same FAQs?
    • Too many follow-up emails?
  2. Design a micro-workflow:
    • Intake: Google Form → Google Sheet
    • Processing: ChatGPT summarizes, decides, or drafts a reply
    • Output: n8n sends the email back to your customer
  3. Ship your v0.
    • It doesn't need to be pretty.
    • You're building a proof of motion, not a final product.
    • Once you've done it once, you'll start seeing loops everywhere.

This is the most basic AI automation stack you can build — and it's enough to open the door to everything else.

The Entry Stack

  1. ChatGPT / GPT-5
    The brain of your operation. Drafts text, makes decisions, summarizes info.
  2. n8n
    The glue. Moves data from one step to the next without you writing a single line of code.
  3. Google Sheets
    Your lightweight database and audit log. Cheap, flexible, and easy to understand.

This trio is your printing press starter kit. Learn it well, and you can build more complex stacks later.

What to Avoid

  • Paralysis by analysis
    AI evolves daily. If you're waiting for things to "stop changing," you'll be left behind.
  • Tool overload
    Every day, someone slaps a new label on an old AI tool and sells it on Facebook.
    Don't try to learn everything. Pick a few impactful tools (like the stack above) and master them.

The Bottom Line

The printing press didn't just make more books — it triggered revolutions in religion, science, business, and language.

AI is our printing press moment.

You don't have to wait for permission from a big company, a tech team, or a "perfect plan."

You just have to build the first loop.

Don't hire a poet — buy a press.
Don't read about change — be the change.
Ship one useful loop this week. Then another. And another.

Access beats elites — every time.

posts.title: How to Automate Customer Onboarding in 30 Minutes
posts.subtitle: Stop manually sending welcome emails and start automating your onboarding process with these simple steps.
posts.description: Stop manually sending welcome emails and start automating your onboarding process with these simple steps that will save you hours every month.
posts.content:
How to Automate Customer Onboarding in 30 Minutes

Stop manually sending welcome emails and start automating your onboarding process with these simple steps.

Why Onboarding Matters More Than You Think

Customer onboarding isn't just "sending a welcome email." It's the first real moment a customer experiences your business after saying yes.

A good onboarding process:

  • Sets expectations clearly so customers know what comes next.
  • Reduces confusion and prevents unnecessary support tickets.
  • Builds trust, making them feel confident they made the right choice.
  • Increases retention rates and customer lifetime value.

A bad onboarding process:

  • Leaves customers wondering if you even know they signed up.
  • Creates delays that frustrate them before they've even started.
  • Leads to churn — sometimes before they've ever used what they paid for.

The good news: you can automate the entire basic onboarding process in under 30 minutes — without hiring a developer or paying for complicated systems.

The Goal: One Loop That Runs Itself

Here's the simple loop we're building:

  1. Trigger: A customer signs up or makes a purchase.
  2. Automated Welcome Email: A warm greeting and clear next steps.
  3. Follow-Up Email: A friendly check-in and helpful resources a few days later.
  4. Optional Personal Touch: A reminder for you or your team to reach out personally.

Think of it as putting your best "first impression" on autopilot.

Pro Tip: Start small. You can always add more emails or steps later. The goal here is to replace the manual "copy-paste welcome email" with something that runs 24/7.

What You'll Need (No-Code Setup)

We're keeping it beginner-friendly with a minimal stack:

  • Trigger Source: Your CRM, website form, or e-commerce checkout (Shopify, WooCommerce, Stripe, etc.).
  • Automation Tool: n8n (free, flexible) or Zapier (easier for beginners, but paid tiers for multi-step workflows).
  • Email Sending Tool: Gmail, Outlook, or a lightweight email marketing platform like MailerLite or ConvertKit.
  • Template Content: A ready-made welcome email and follow-up email copy.

Step 1: Map the Customer Journey (5 Minutes)

Before opening any software, decide what needs to happen after someone becomes a customer.

Ask yourself:

  • What's the very first thing they need to know or do?
  • What's the one action that would make them feel confident about their purchase?
  • What resources would help them get started quickly?
  • When should you follow up to check on their progress?

Write this down in simple steps. Don't overthink it — you can refine later.

Step 2: Create Your Email Templates (10 Minutes)

Create two email templates:

Welcome Email Template

Subject: Welcome to [Your Business]! Here's what's next...

Body:

Hi [Name],

Welcome to [Your Business]! We're excited to have you on board.

Here's what happens next:

  • Step 1: [Specific action they should take]
  • Step 2: [Next action]
  • Step 3: [Final action]

If you have any questions, just reply to this email. We're here to help!

Best regards,
[Your Name]
[Your Business]

Follow-Up Email Template

Subject: How's it going with [Your Business]?

Body:

Hi [Name],

It's been a few days since you joined [Your Business]. How are things going?

If you've run into any issues or have questions, don't hesitate to reach out. We want to make sure you're getting the most out of [Your Product/Service].

Here are some helpful resources:

  • [Resource 1]
  • [Resource 2]
  • [Resource 3]

Looking forward to hearing from you!

Best regards,
[Your Name]

Step 3: Set Up Your Automation (15 Minutes)

Now let's connect everything:

Option A: Using n8n (Free)

  1. Sign up for n8n.cloud (free tier)
  2. Create a new workflow
  3. Add your trigger (Google Sheets, webhook, etc.)
  4. Add an email node (Gmail, SMTP, etc.)
  5. Configure your welcome email template
  6. Add a delay node (3-5 days)
  7. Add another email node for your follow-up
  8. Test and activate

Option B: Using Zapier (Paid)

  1. Create a new Zap
  2. Choose your trigger app
  3. Set up your welcome email action
  4. Add a delay step
  5. Set up your follow-up email action
  6. Test and turn on

Step 4: Test and Refine (5 Minutes)

Before going live:

  1. Test the full flow with your own email
  2. Check that all personalization works correctly
  3. Verify timing between emails
  4. Make sure your email templates look good on mobile

Then activate and let it run!

Pro Tips for Success

  • Keep it personal: Use their name and reference their specific purchase or signup.
  • Set clear expectations: Tell them exactly what to expect and when.
  • Make it easy to get help: Provide multiple ways to contact you.
  • Track what works: Monitor open rates and responses to improve your templates.
  • Start simple: You can always add more sophisticated automation later.

What to Measure

Track these metrics to see if your automation is working:

  • Email open rates: Are people reading your welcome emails?
  • Response rates: Are customers engaging with your follow-ups?
  • Support ticket volume: Are fewer people asking basic questions?
  • Customer satisfaction: Are new customers happier with their experience?
  • Retention rates: Are customers sticking around longer?

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Over-automating: Don't send too many emails too quickly.
  • Generic content: Make sure your emails feel personal and relevant.
  • Ignoring feedback: Pay attention to customer responses and adjust accordingly.
  • Setting and forgetting: Regularly review and update your automation.

Next Steps

Once you have this basic automation running, you can expand to:

  • Product usage tracking and personalized recommendations
  • Milestone celebrations (30 days, 100 days, etc.)
  • Re-engagement campaigns for inactive customers
  • Upsell and cross-sell automation
  • Customer feedback collection

The Bottom Line

Automating your customer onboarding doesn't have to be complicated or expensive.

Start with this simple 30-minute setup, and you'll immediately see:

  • Less manual work for you and your team
  • Happier, more confident customers
  • Better retention rates
  • More time to focus on growing your business

The key is to start small, test everything, and iterate based on what works for your specific customers.

Remember: the goal isn't to replace human connection — it's to handle the routine tasks so you can focus on the meaningful interactions that really matter.
